question_type_names: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students judge a source's usefulness purely by who wrote it ('biased therefore not useful'), instead of weighing content, provenance and contextual knowledge together.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: AQA principal examiner reports on GCSE History 8145 source-utility questions; Pearson GCSE History sources and interpretations guide

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students write 'first X happened, then Y, then Z' chronologies with no causal links between events, and so cannot reach the top mark band.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: OUP Education blog summary of AQA GCSE History examiner reports; AQA principal examiner reports on Paper 1 Section B narrative-account questions

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students confuse 'why interpretations differ' (focus on authors, evidence, purpose, time of writing) with 'how they differ' (focus on what each one says) and answer the wrong question.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: AQA principal examiner reports on GCSE History 8145 Paper 1 Section A interpretation questions

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students treat 'significance' as a synonym for 'importance at the time' and ignore importance over time, which is needed for full marks on the 8-mark thematic question.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: AQA principal examiner reports on GCSE History 8145 Paper 2 Section A significance questions

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students answer extended-response questions in the first person or as a diary entry, which prevents them meeting the AO2 analytical-link descriptors.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: AQA principal examiner reports flagging this as a recurring issue across multiple series

common_misconceptions_subject_wide.misconception: Students list factors one after another (war, religion, government...) without weighing the stated factor against the others, missing the judgement required by AO2.
common_misconceptions_subject_wide.source: AQA principal examiner reports on GCSE History 8145 Paper 2 Section A factor essays

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: Top-band source-utility responses always integrate all three of content, provenance and the student's own contextual knowledge — not two of the three.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: AQA examiner report guidance on Paper 1 Section B and Paper 2 Section A source-utility questions

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: The 16-mark historic environment essay rewards explicit links between the specified site and wider events of the period; describing the site without linking back loses marks.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.2 for Paper 2 Section B

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: On 12-mark bullet-format essays in Period Studies, the highest-band answers reach a substantiated overall judgement rather than just covering both bullet points.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: AQA scheme of assessment 4.4.1 and principal examiner commentary on Paper 1 Section A

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: SPaG marks (4) on each paper reward consistent accuracy and a wide range of specialist historical terms — students who avoid historical vocabulary cap themselves at the threshold band.
examiner_signals_subject_wide.source: AQA spec section 4.4.3 SPaG performance descriptors

examiner_signals_subject_wide.signal: AO weighting tilts towards AO1/AO2 (35% each) over AO3/AO4 (15% each); knowledge and analysis matter more than source/interpretation work over the full course.

spec_changes_2026.change: Specified historic environment sites are updated for the 2026-2028 cycle in each of the four British depth study options. Site names are released by AQA three years in advance and downstream per-option planners must use the 2026 site for that option.

No subject-content changes for 2026 — the spec remains the version dated 24 September 2019 (version 1.3); the assessment structure of Paper 1 (84 marks, two hours) and Paper 2 (84 marks, two hours) is unchanged.

pedagogical_notes_history_specific.note: EEF Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools recommends explicit teaching of disciplinary vocabulary — for History this means front-loading second-order concepts (cause, consequence, change, continuity, similarity, difference, significance) so students can deploy them in extended responses.
pedagogical_notes_history_specific.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Improving Literacy in Secondary Schools guidance report

pedagogical_notes_history_specific.note: EEF Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning recommends modelling expert thinking — for source/interpretation questions this means teachers walking through how they decide content vs provenance vs context, not just giving students a checklist.
pedagogical_notes_history_specific.source: Education Endowment Foundation, Metacognition and Self-Regulated Learning guidance report

pedagogical_notes_history_specific.note: Cambridge Assessment research on history examinations highlights that comparative judgement (comparing causes, consequences, factors) is consistently the hardest skill for GCSE candidates — schedule extra retrieval and worked examples on every comparison or judgement question type.
pedagogical_notes_history_specific.source: Cambridge Assessment Network and Research, history specifications and reports archive

pedagogical_notes_history_specific.note: AQA's own course-design rationale notes that the British 40% can be taught in any order — it works well to teach the thematic study around the British depth study chronologically, so the depth period sits inside the longer sweep.
pedagogical_notes_history_specific.source: AQA spec section 3.1 rationale and course-design guidance

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: The past is a foreign country: they do things differently there.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: L.P. Hartley

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: History is not the past. It is the method we have evolved of organising our ignorance of the past.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Hilary Mantel

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: George Santayana

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: The history of the world is but the biography of great men.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Thomas Carlyle

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: Study the historian before you begin to study the facts.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: E.H. Carr

quote_ticker_quotes.quote: History will be kind to me for I intend to write it.
quote_ticker_quotes.author: Winston Churchill
